title: Scaling mechanics
summary: How to grow a profitable campaign without breaking it: when to scale, how big each step should be, when to duplicate, and how to open new audiences, geos and creatives. You will judge every step by confirmed CPA since the step and marginal profit, using the same starting rules as the Budget and kill rules module, and finish with a two-week worked case.

lessons.title: Is it ready to scale?
objectives: By the end you can tell a campaign that is ready to scale from one that only had a lucky week.
By the end you can calculate margin headroom and cash runway before adding budget.
By the end you can list the situations where the right answer is not to scale.

steps.p: Testing asks one question: does this work at all? Scaling asks a harder one: how much more money can this absorb before the cost per result rises past what you earn? Many profitable campaigns die at the scaling step, not the testing step, because the buyer adds money faster than the data can support.

d.b: Testing finds it. Scaling stretches it.

steps.say: Here's the big idea on screen: testing finds it, scaling stretches it. When you test, you're asking one question. Does this work at all? Scaling asks a harder one. How much more money can this campaign absorb before the cost per result climbs past what you earn? Many profitable campaigns die right here, at the scaling step, not the testing step. Why? Because the buyer adds money faster than the data can support. So scaling needs its own rules.

steps.h: Four signals a campaign is ready
steps.p: A campaign is ready when four things are true at the same time. One strong signal on its own, like a single cheap day, is not enough. Check all four before you touch the budget.
d: Volume|enough conversions to trust the average
Stability|cost per result steady for several days
Capacity|offer cap and your cash can take more
steps.say: Look at these four cards. A campaign is ready to scale when all four are true at the same time. Volume, meaning enough conversions to trust the average. Stability, meaning the cost per result has held steady for several days. Headroom, meaning your C P A, cost per acquisition, sits well below the payout. And capacity, meaning the offer cap and your own cash can take more. One strong signal on its own, like a single cheap day, isn't enough. Check all four before you touch the budget.

steps.p: Headroom tells you how much room you have before scaling eats your profit. Scaling almost always raises cost per result, so headroom is the buffer that absorbs that rise.
steps.more: CPA here means your real cost per confirmed result, such as cost per FTD (first-time deposit) confirmed by the network, not the number the ad platform reports. A campaign with thin headroom can be profitable at its current budget and still be a poor candidate for scaling, because any rise in cost wipes out the margin.
steps.say: Here's the headroom formula. Take the payout, subtract your C P A, then divide by the payout. Headroom tells you how much room you have before scaling eats your profit. Scaling almost always raises cost per result, so headroom is the buffer that absorbs that rise. One important detail. C P A here means your real cost per confirmed result, such as cost per F T D, first-time deposit, confirmed by the network, not the number the ad platform reports. Thin headroom can be profitable today and still be a poor candidate for scaling.

steps.p: Example: the network pays $50 per qualified FTD. Over the last 7 days your confirmed cost per FTD is $30. Headroom is (50 − 30) ÷ 50 = 0.40, or 40%. Your CPA could rise to almost $50 before you stop making money on each extra FTD.
steps.more: Compare a second campaign: payout $50, CPA $44. Headroom is (50 − 44) ÷ 50 = 12%. Both campaigns are profitable today. Only the first one has room to scale. A rough guide many operators use is to want 30% or more headroom before scaling hard, but this varies by geo, vertical and how fast payouts arrive.
steps.say: Let's work an example. The network pays fifty dollars per qualified F T D. Over the last seven days, your confirmed cost per F T D is thirty dollars. Fifty minus thirty is twenty, divided by fifty, gives forty percent headroom, the number on screen. Your C P A could rise to almost fifty dollars before each extra F T D stops making money. Now compare a campaign paying fifty with a C P A of forty four. That's only twelve percent. Both are profitable today, but only the first has room to scale. Many operators want thirty percent or more, though it varies by geo, vertical and payout speed.

steps.h: Headroom and the rule card agree
steps.p: Example: payout $50 and the 25% margin used in the Budget and kill rules module. Your target CPA is $37.50 and your scale line, 0.8 × target, is $30. A campaign sitting at the scale line has exactly 40% headroom, so the two checks point the same way. Starting rules; adapt them to your vertical and data.
steps.more: Check the maths: 50 × 0.75 = 37.50. 0.8 × 37.50 = 30. 2 × 37.50 = 75. 1.5 × 37.50 = 56.25, which is above the $50 payout, so the CPA kill line is the lower number, $50. Headroom at the scale line: (50 − 30) ÷ 50 = 40%. Count only network-confirmed conversions. Full rules and timing: Budget and kill rules module.
steps.say: This table shows that headroom and the rule card agree. Example: a fifty dollar payout and the twenty five percent margin from the Budget and kill rules module. The target C P A is thirty seven dollars fifty, and the scale line, zero point eight times target, is thirty dollars. Read down the rows. Break-even is fifty. The zero-F T D kill is seventy five. The C P A kill line is the lower of one point five times target and break-even, so fifty. A campaign at the thirty dollar scale line has exactly forty percent headroom. These are starting rules, so adapt them, and count only network-confirmed conversions.

steps.h: Lab: does it pass the scale row?
steps.p: Apply the rule card before you think about bigger moves. Work out the confirmed CPA, compare it with the $30 scale line and count the conversions. Then use the readiness table on the next slide for anything bigger than one +20% step.

steps.p: Use this as a starting point, not a law. One +20% step only needs the scale row of the rule card. The rough guides below are for bigger moves: larger steps, duplicates and new geos. They vary by geo, vertical and payout size, so write your own down before you look at the data.

No point buying FTDs you cannot sell

steps.say: This readiness checklist is a starting point, not a law. One plus twenty percent step only needs the scale row of the rule card. These rough guides are for bigger moves, like larger steps, duplicates and new geos. Look down the rows. Fifteen to thirty conversions in three to seven days, because small samples lie. A C P A trend that's flat or falling. Headroom of thirty percent or more. Frequency still low. The offer cap under seventy percent used. And cash runway that covers the payout delay. These vary by geo, vertical and payout size, so write your own down before you look at the data.

steps.p: Illustration: two campaigns with the same 7-day average CPA of about $23.60. The first is stable. The second swings wildly. Only the first gives you a reliable base to scale from. The second needs more data or a fix first.
steps.more: Both lines add up to $165 over 7 days, so both average $23.57. The noisy campaign often has too few conversions per day, so one or two FTDs more or less moves the CPA a lot. The fix is usually patience or consolidation, not more budget.

steps.p: Example: you plan to scale to $400 a day. The network pays monthly, about 30 days after month end, so you may spend for 45 days or more before the first payout lands. That is $18,000 of your own cash in the system before money comes back.
steps.more: At $100 a day the same delay needs $4,500. Scaling four times means four times the cash tied up. Payment terms vary by network and are sometimes negotiable once you have history. Many operators who were profitable on paper have stopped because they ran out of cash, not because the campaign stopped working.
steps.say: Now cash runway. Example: you plan to scale to four hundred dollars a day. The network pays monthly, about thirty days after month end, so you may spend for forty five days or more before the first payout lands. That's eighteen thousand dollars, the number on screen, of your own cash in the system before money comes back. At one hundred dollars a day, the same delay needs four thousand five hundred. Payment terms vary by network. Many operators who were profitable on paper stopped because they ran out of cash, not because the campaign stopped working.

steps.p: Put the evidence side by side. If most of what you see sits in the right column, waiting is the profitable choice, even if it feels slow.
steps.say: Put the evidence side by side. On the left, ready: C P A steady for five or more days, headroom above thirty percent, the network confirms quality, and the cap and cash have room. On the right, not yet: one great day, a C P A close to the payout, the network flagged your traffic, or cash that only covers a week. If most of what you see sits in the right column, waiting is the profitable choice, even if it feels slow.

steps.p: These four mistakes cause most of the failed scaling attempts we see. Each one makes a campaign look more ready than it really is. Check yourself against the left column every time you open the readiness sheet.

items: No cash for the payout delay

b.title: Fixes

Fund 45 days at the new budget

steps.say: These four mistakes cause most failed scaling attempts, and each one makes a campaign look more ready than it really is. Counting platform conversions, fixed by using network-confirmed F T Ds only. Scaling on one cheap day, fixed by judging three to seven days of data. Forgetting the offer cap, fixed by asking the manager about the cap first. And no cash for the payout delay, fixed by funding forty five days at the new budget. Check yourself against the left column every time you open your readiness sheet.

steps.p: Some situations mean you should not scale, however good the numbers look on the dashboard. Treat any one of these as a stop sign until it is resolved.
d: CPA has risen three days in a row
The offer cap is nearly full
The ad account is under review
Cash will not cover the payout delay
Only one ad is carrying all results
steps.say: Some situations mean you should not scale, however good the dashboard looks. Read through this list. C P A has risen three days in a row. The offer cap is nearly full. The network questioned your traffic quality. The ad account is under review. Cash won't cover the payout delay. Or only one ad is carrying all the results. Treat any one of these as a stop sign until it's resolved.

steps.p: Networks check the quality of what you send. If deposits are tiny, users are duplicates or activity looks unusual, they can hold or reverse payouts. Scaling low-quality traffic multiplies that problem.

d.text: Ask your manager for quality feedback before you scale. A reversal after scaling hurts far more than one before.

steps.say: A word on quality. Networks check the quality of what you send. If deposits are tiny, users are duplicates, or activity looks unusual, they can hold or reverse payouts. Scaling low-quality traffic just multiplies that problem. So, as the warning on screen says, ask your manager for quality feedback before you scale. A reversal after scaling hurts far more than one before.

steps.h: A readiness review in five steps
steps.p: Run this short review before every budget increase, in the same order each time. It takes about ten minutes and it stops most of the expensive mistakes buyers make when a campaign feels hot.
steps.say: Here's a short readiness review. Follow the flow on screen. Pull your seven-day data. Check the C P A trend. Calculate headroom. Check the cap and your cash. Get quality feedback from the network. Then decide the step. Run it before every budget increase, in the same order each time. It takes about ten minutes, and it stops most of the expensive mistakes buyers make when a campaign feels hot.

steps.p: When you are unsure, waiting a day costs little. Scaling a campaign that was never stable can cost a week of profit. Good operators are patient at this step and fast at the next ones.

takeaways: Scaling asks how much more money a campaign can absorb, not just whether it works.
Check volume, stability, headroom and capacity together before adding budget.
Cash runway and payout delays limit how fast you can scale, even when the campaign is profitable.

quiz.q: Payout is $40 and confirmed CPA is $30. What is the headroom?
quiz.why: Headroom is (40 − 30) ÷ 40 = 0.25, or 25%. 33% divides by the CPA instead of the payout.

quiz.q: Two campaigns both average $24 CPA over 7 days. Which is the better scaling candidate?
options: The one whose daily CPA is steady
The one whose daily CPA swings the most
The one with the most clicks
Either, since the average is the same
quiz.why: A steady CPA gives a reliable base. Large swings usually mean too few conversions to trust the average.

options: The network questioned your traffic quality
CPA is flat for a week
quiz.why: Scaling traffic the network doubts multiplies the risk of held or reversed payouts. The other options are healthy signs.

quiz.q: You want to spend $250 a day and payouts arrive about 40 days after spend. Roughly how much cash must you fund?
quiz.why: $250 × 40 days = $10,000 of spend before the first payout arrives.

lessons.title: Vertical scaling: more budget, same setup
objectives: By the end you can raise budget in steps that keep cost per result stable.
By the end you can calculate marginal CPA and use it to decide the next step.
By the end you can explain how large budget changes interact with the learning phase.

steps.p: Vertical scaling means putting more money into the same campaign, ad set and ads. Nothing else changes. It is the simplest way to grow, and the fastest way to break a winner if you do it carelessly.

d.s: Simple to do, easy to overdo

steps.say: Vertical scaling means putting more money into the same campaign, ad set and ads. Nothing else changes. As the screen says, same setup, more money. It's the simplest way to grow, and that's exactly why it's so easy to overdo. Done carelessly, it's also the fastest way to break a winner. In this lesson, we'll learn how to add money without breaking what already works.

steps.p: Example: a ladder of +20% steps from $50 a day, the starting rule from the Budget and kill rules module. Each step must be earned again with fresh data and waits at least 48 hours before the next. Four steps take you from $50 to about $104 a day.
steps.more: Check the maths: 50 × 1.2 = 60. 60 × 1.2 = 72. 72 × 1.2 = 86.40. 86.40 × 1.2 = 103.68, about $104. With at least 48 hours between steps, four steps take at least 8 days, and longer when a step has to wait for data. That feels slow, but a campaign that holds its CPA at $104 a day is worth far more than one that breaks at $100 after one big jump.
steps.say: Here's an example budget ladder. Start at fifty dollars a day, and each step adds twenty percent, the starting rule from the Budget and kill rules module. Fifty becomes sixty, then seventy two, then about eighty six, then about one hundred and four. Each step must be earned again with fresh data, and waits at least forty eight hours before the next. So four steps take at least eight days. That feels slow, but a campaign that holds its C P A, cost per acquisition, at one hundred and four dollars a day is worth far more than one that breaks after one big jump.

steps.p: There is no perfect step size. Bigger steps get you there faster and carry more risk of a cost spike. Our starting rule is +20%. A bigger step of +30% to 50% is only for CPA at or under 0.6 × target with at least 10 confirmed conversions. Rough guide; varies by account and vertical.
steps.say: There's no perfect step size. Look at the rows. Ten to twenty percent is slow, with low risk of a cost spike, and twenty percent is our starting rule. Thirty to fifty percent is fast, with high risk, and it's for advanced buyers only. Doubling or more is very fast and very high risk. A bigger step of thirty to fifty percent is only for a C P A at or under zero point six times target, with at least ten confirmed conversions. This is a rough guide, and it varies by account and vertical.

steps.p: On Meta, a significant edit to an ad set, which can include a large budget change, may send it back into the learning phase, where delivery and cost are less stable. We are not certain of the current threshold, and the +20% step is a habit, not an official number. Check Meta's Help Center.

steps.p: Illustration: CPA after seven budget changes. Steady steps let cost drift up slowly. Big jumps cause spikes, then partial recovery, and the buyer often panics and cuts at the worst moment.
steps.say: This is an illustration of C P A after seven budget changes. Look at the steady line, twenty percent steps. Cost drifts up slowly, from twenty two to twenty six dollars. Now the other line, big jumps. It spikes, partly recovers, then spikes again, up to thirty eight. And here's the human problem. The buyer often panics and cuts at the worst moment. Steady steps give you a calmer line, and calmer decisions.

steps.p: Your average CPA hides what the extra money is buying. Marginal CPA measures the cost of only the additional results you got from the additional spend. It is the number that tells you whether the last step was worth it.
steps.say: Here's a formula that changes how you scale. Extra spend, divided by extra F T Ds, that's first-time deposits, equals marginal C P A. Your average C P A hides what the extra money is buying. Marginal C P A measures the cost of only the additional results you got from the additional spend. It's the number that tells you whether your last step was actually worth it.

steps.p: Example: at $300 a day, CPA is $20, so you get 15 FTDs. You scale to $450 a day and CPA rises to $24, so you get 18.75 FTDs on average. The extra $150 bought 3.75 extra FTDs. That is $40 each.
steps.more: The average only moved from $20 to $24, which looks fine. But every FTD the new money bought cost $40. If your payout is $45, the extra spend is barely profitable: $5 of margin per extra FTD against $25 at the original budget. If the payout were $35, the step lost money even though the average CPA of $24 still looks profitable.
steps.say: Let's work it. Example: at three hundred dollars a day, C P A is twenty, so you get fifteen F T Ds. You scale to four hundred and fifty a day, and C P A rises to twenty four, so you get eighteen point seven five F T Ds on average. The extra one hundred and fifty dollars bought three point seven five extra F T Ds. That's forty dollars each, the number on screen. The average only moved from twenty to twenty four, which looks fine. But with a forty five dollar payout, the extra spend is barely profitable. With a thirty five dollar payout, that step lost money.

steps.p: Example from the last slide, with a $45 payout. The average CPA looks comfortable. The marginal CPA shows the new money is working much harder for much less.
steps.say: Here's the same example as bars, with a forty five dollar payout. The first bar, average C P A at three hundred a day, twenty dollars. Next, the average at four hundred and fifty a day, twenty four. Now look at the third bar, the marginal C P A of the extra money, forty dollars, sitting right up near the payout bar at forty five. The average looks comfortable. The marginal shows the new money is working much harder for much less.

steps.say: These are the step rules after each twenty percent step. Example: payout forty, target thirty, scale line twenty four. Judge only the spend and conversions since the step, not the lifetime total. Read the rows. Forty eight hours or more, two or more F T Ds, and C P A at or under twenty four, take the next step. Between twenty four and thirty, keep, with no more steps. Above thirty for forty eight hours, back to the last good budget. Above forty, which is break-even, back one step now. And if the cap is nearly full, stop raising. Count network-confirmed F T Ds only.

steps.p: Judge the numbers since the step, not the lifetime total. Work out the CPA since the step and compare it with the $24 scale line and the $30 target. In the tool, Keep shows as Hold, because the action is the same: no budget change.

steps.h: Never scale to recover a bad day
steps.p: Raising budget to win back yesterday's loss is a gambler's move. The campaign does not know you lost money. Decide on the data trend, not on how you feel.

d.text: If the trend is bad, the answer is hold or roll back, never add.

steps.say: One last rule. Never scale to recover a bad day. Raising budget to win back yesterday's loss is a gambler's move. The campaign doesn't know you lost money. quiz.why: $200 bought 10 FTDs; $300 bought 12. The extra $100 bought 2 FTDs, so $50 each.

quiz.q: Your ad set runs at $60 a day and has earned its next step. Under the starting rule, what is the new daily budget?
quiz.why: The starting rule is +20%: $60 × 1.2 = $72. Bigger steps are reserved for CPA at or under 0.6 × target with 10+ conversions.

quiz.q: You raised budget yesterday and today CPA is high. What is usually the right first move?
options: Raise budget again to push through
Change the creative and audience as well
Wait for the change to settle unless losses pass your rule
quiz.why: One day after a change is too early to judge. Wait unless a pre-set loss rule is hit, and never stack changes.

quiz.q: Payout is $35. Average CPA rose from $20 to $25 after scaling, and marginal CPA is $40. What does this mean?
options: The step is profitable because $25 is below $35
The extra spend is losing money on each extra FTD
quiz.why: Each extra FTD costs $40 against a $35 payout. The average hides this loss.

quiz.q: Why might a campaign with a cost cap not spend its full budget?
options: The platform cannot find enough results near the cap
quiz.why: A cap limits cost. If few results are available at that price, spend stays below budget.

lessons.say_intro: This lesson is about vertical scaling, adding budget to the same setup. You'll learn to raise budget in steps that keep cost stable, and to measure what the extra money is really buying, so you can decide your next step with confidence.
lessons.say_outro: So, vertical scaling means small, earned steps, one change at a time, judged on C P A since the step and on marginal cost. Your task: for your best campaign, write a five-step budget ladder with twenty percent steps, and the date you'll check each step. Now take the quiz.

lessons.title: Duplication and campaign structure
objectives: By the end you can use duplication on purpose instead of as a reflex.
By the end you can set up a testing and scaling structure with clear naming.
By the end you can compare a duplicate against its parent fairly.

steps.h: Duplication is a tool, not a fix
steps.p: Duplicating means copying a campaign or ad set and running the copy alongside or instead of the original. It can help you scale. It can also split your data, confuse your reporting and hide the real reason something stopped working.

d.s: Every duplicate needs a job and an end date

steps.say: Duplicating means copying a campaign or ad set and running the copy alongside, or instead of, the original. It can help you scale. But it can also split your data, confuse your reporting, and hide the real reason something stopped working. That's why the screen says, copy with a reason. Every duplicate needs a job, and an end date.

steps.p: Each reason gives the duplicate a different job. Write that job in your notes before you create the copy, so you know what success means. Under our starting rules a duplicate begins at the original's start budget, not its raised budget, and is judged from zero.
d: Scale beside the winner|copy at the start budget
New bidding|same setup, different bid strategy
steps.say: Here are four reasons to duplicate, and each one gives the copy a different job. Scale beside the winner, copying at the start budget. New audience, same ads but different people. New geo, the same angle in a new country. And new bidding, the same setup with a different bid strategy. Write the job in your notes before you create the copy, so you know what success means. Under our starting rules, a duplicate begins at the original's start budget, not its raised budget, and it's judged from zero.

steps.p: Many teams separate testing from scaling. New ideas start cheap in a testing campaign. Winners graduate to a scaling campaign with more budget. Losers are switched off and recorded, not deleted.
steps.more: Separating the two keeps small tests from stealing budget from proven winners, and keeps proven winners from being disturbed by constant testing. Do not delete losing ads: switch them off and keep the record, so you never pay to test the same failed idea twice.
steps.say: Many teams separate testing from scaling. Follow the flow. New ideas start cheap in a testing campaign. You pick the winners. Winners graduate to a scaling campaign with more budget, where you monitor and refresh them. And losers are archived with notes. This keeps small tests from stealing budget from proven winners, and keeps winners from being disturbed by constant testing. Don't delete losing ads. Switch them off and keep the record, so you never pay to test the same failed idea twice.

steps.p: Names are how a team reads an account at a glance. Pick one pattern and use it everywhere: campaigns, ad sets, ads, tracker and sheet. Example pattern below.
steps.more: Full example: NG_META_OFR12_PROOF_SCALE_1004. Anyone on the team can now filter the account, the tracker and the sheet by any part of the name. Keep the parent's name in the duplicate with a suffix, like _D1, so you can always trace where it came from.
steps.say: Names are how a team reads an account at a glance. Here's an example pattern. The geo, like N G for Nigeria. The traffic source, like Meta. The offer I D from your sheet. The creative angle, like proof. The stage, test or scale. And the launch date. Pick one pattern and use it everywhere: campaigns, ad sets, ads, tracker and sheet. Then anyone on the team can filter by any part of the name. And keep the parent's name in a duplicate, with a suffix like D one, so you can always trace where it came from.

steps.p: Example: one angle's life in names. It starts in testing, graduates to scaling, gets one duplicate, then a test in Kenya. Anyone on the team can filter the account, the tracker and the sheet by geo, offer, angle or stage without asking you.

d.note: Parent name plus _D1 shows where every copy came from.

steps.say: Here's one angle's life in names, the text on screen. It starts in testing, in Nigeria. A few days later it graduates to scaling. Then it gets one duplicate, marked with D one at the end. Then it gets a test in Kenya, with K E at the front. Notice how the parent name plus that D one suffix shows where every copy came from. Anyone on the team can filter the account, the tracker and the sheet by geo, offer, angle or stage, without asking you.

steps.p: A few simple rules keep duplication from turning the account into a mess that nobody, including you in three weeks from now, can read or trust.
d: Only after the original passed 2 steps
Start at the original start budget
At most 2 copies per winner at once
Record the parent and the reason
steps.say: A few simple rules keep duplication from turning your account into a mess. Only duplicate after the original has passed two steps. Start the copy at the original start budget. Leave the original untouched. Keep at most two copies per winner at once. Record the parent and the reason. And judge each copy from zero. Follow these, and the account stays readable, including for you, three weeks from now.

steps.p: Generic mock-ups, not real screens. The duplicate option and its menus change, and we are not certain these names are current, so check the current Ads Manager. The order is what matters: copy, place, rename, set the start budget, log.

steps.text: Tick the winning ad set and choose Duplicate. Do not edit the original.

steps.title: Choose where it goes
steps.text: Send the copy to your scaling campaign. Keep the ads and audience the same unless the copy's job is a new audience.

steps.title: Rename and set the start budget
steps.text: Add _D1 to the parent name and set the original start budget, $40, not the raised $80.

steps.title: Log the copy
steps.text: Write the parent, the reason, the start budget and the date. The copy now runs its own rule card from zero.

steps.p: Example: target $30, break-even $40. A duplicate is a new ad set, so it gets the full rule card from zero, with its own checkpoints and its own spend. Starting rules from the Budget and kill rules module; adapt them to your vertical and data.
steps.say: How do you judge a duplicate? Example: target thirty, break-even forty. A duplicate is a new ad set, so it gets the full rule card from zero, with its own checkpoints and its own spend. Zero F T Ds, first-time deposits, at sixty dollars spent, kill the copy. Ninety dollars or more spent with a C P A, cost per acquisition, over forty, kill it. Three or more F T Ds at or under twenty four, take a twenty percent step, forty eight hours apart. Between twenty four and thirty, keep. Anything else, hold. These are starting rules, so adapt them to your vertical and data.

steps.h: Worked example: a duplicate beside the winner
steps.p: Example: a winner started at $40 a day and has been stepped up to $80 at $18 CPA, target $30. You duplicate it into the scaling campaign at its $40 start budget and leave the original running. After 3 days the copy runs at $21 CPA, under the $24 scale line, so it stays.
steps.say: Let's work an example. A winner started at forty dollars a day and has been stepped up to eighty, at an eighteen dollar C P A, with a thirty dollar target. You duplicate it into the scaling campaign at its forty dollar start budget, and leave the original running. After three days the copy runs at twenty one dollars, under the twenty four dollar scale line, so it stays. Look at the maths on screen. About four point four F T Ds a day from the original, plus about one point nine from the copy, gives about six point three five a day in total.

steps.p: Example from the last slide. Total spend rose by half, from $80 to $120 a day, and blended CPA moved from $18 to about $18.90. That is a healthy result. If the copy keeps earning its own +20% steps, it climbs the ladder just as the original did.
steps.say: Following on from that example, total spend rose by half, from eighty to one hundred and twenty dollars a day. And the blended C P A, the number on screen, moved from eighteen dollars to about eighteen ninety. That's one hundred and twenty divided by six point three five F T Ds. A small rise for fifty percent more spend is a healthy result. If the copy keeps earning its own twenty percent steps, it climbs the ladder just as the original did.

steps.p: Example: three copies of the same winner after equal spend. Identical setups often perform differently because they enter different auctions and find different early users. Judge each copy on its own results.
steps.more: Bar length is CPA on a $50 scale. With a $30 target and a $40 payout, the CPA kill line is $40. Copy B has spent the same as the others, more than 3 × target, at $44 CPA, so the rule card says kill it. Do not keep making copies until one gets lucky: that is gambling with the budget and it fills the account with clutter.
steps.say: Not every copy wins. Example: three copies of the same winner, after equal spend. Bar length is C P A. The original sits at eighteen dollars. Copy A, twenty one. Copy C, nineteen. But look at copy B, forty four dollars. Identical setups often perform differently, because they enter different auctions and find different early users. With a forty dollar kill line, copy B has spent more than three times target, so the rule card says kill it. And don't keep making copies until one gets lucky. That's gambling with the budget, and it fills the account with clutter.

steps.p: A rough guide: fewer ad sets with more budget each tend to learn faster than many small ones, because each gets more conversions to learn from. Varies by platform and account.

b.title: Consolidated
items: Each gets several FTDs a day

steps.say: Here's a rough guide on structure. On the left, fragmented: twelve ad sets at ten dollars each, each getting zero to one F T D a day, with slow, noisy learning and results that are hard to read. On the right, consolidated: three ad sets at forty dollars, each getting several F T Ds a day, with faster, steadier learning and clear results. Fewer ad sets with more budget each tend to learn faster, because each gets more conversions to learn from. This varies by platform and account.

steps.p: Most failed duplicates fail for the same few reasons. Each mistake on the left either overspends the copy or misreads it. The fixes on the right match the rules in the Budget and kill rules module.

a.title: Mistakes
items: Judging the copy on the parent's history
Many copies to find a lucky one
Killing the original when a copy fails

steps.say: Most failed duplicates fail for the same few reasons. Copying at the raised budget, fixed by starting at the start budget. Judging the copy on the parent's history, fixed by using the rule card from zero. Making many copies to find a lucky one, fixed by keeping at most two copies at once. And killing the original when a copy fails, fixed by switching off only the failing copy. These fixes match the rules in the Budget and kill rules module.

steps.h: Duplication is not a way past review
steps.p: Copying a rejected ad and relaunching it to slip past review is circumvention. Platforms treat it as a serious policy violation and it can lead to account restrictions.

d.text: If an ad is rejected, fix it or request a review. Never re-upload it unchanged to dodge the decision.

steps.say: This one is a compliance warning, so listen carefully. Copying a rejected ad and relaunching it to slip past review is circumvention. Platforms treat it as a serious policy violation, and it can lead to account restrictions. As the warning on screen says, if an ad is rejected, fix it or request a review. Never re-upload it unchanged to dodge the decision.

steps.h: Structure is how you scale a team
steps.p: A clear structure and naming pattern let a second buyer understand your account without asking you. That matters once you scale beyond what one person can watch.

d.b: If a stranger can read it, it can scale

steps.say: Here's the closing idea: if a stranger can read it, it can scale. A clear structure and naming pattern let a second buyer understand your account without asking you. That matters once you scale beyond what one person can watch. So remember, structure first, budget second.

takeaways: Duplicate with a stated reason and leave the original untouched.
Separate testing from scaling and use one naming convention everywhere.
Compare copies at equal spend and switch off the ones that lose.

quiz.q: An original spends $100 at $20 CPA. A copy spends $100 at $25 CPA. What is the blended CPA?
quiz.why: FTDs are 5 + 4 = 9. $200 ÷ 9 = $22.22. Simply averaging $20 and $25 gives $22.50, which is wrong.

quiz.q: What should you do with the original winner when you create a duplicate?
quiz.why: The original is your proven baseline. Changing it at the same time makes it impossible to tell what caused any change in results.

quiz.q: Copy B costs about double the other copies after equal spend, above the CPA kill line. What do you do?
options: Make more copies until one works
Switch it off and record why
quiz.why: Judge each copy on its own results. Endless copies are gambling and clutter the account.

quiz.q: A winner started at $30 a day and now runs at $52. Under the starting rules, what budget does a new duplicate start at?
quiz.why: A duplicate is a new ad set judged from zero, so it starts at the original start budget, $30, and earns its own steps.

quiz.q: Your ad was rejected. A colleague suggests re-uploading it in a new ad set. What is correct?
options: Fix the ad or request a review instead
Do it in a new ad account
quiz.why: Relaunching to dodge review is circumvention and risks account restrictions. Fix or appeal.

lessons.say_intro: This lesson covers duplication and campaign structure. You'll learn to duplicate on purpose rather than by reflex, to name things so anyone can read your account, and to judge a copy fairly against its parent.
lessons.say_outro: So, duplicate with a reason, start every copy at the start budget, judge it from zero, and name everything so a stranger could follow it. Your task: write your naming convention on one line, and rename the campaigns in one account to match it. Now take the quiz.

lessons.title: Horizontal scaling: audiences, geos, creatives
objectives: By the end you can choose between new audiences, geos, placements, creatives and sources as scaling levers.
By the end you can plan a geo expansion that respects regulation and local differences.
By the end you can keep a creative supply that matches your spend.

steps.p: Vertical scaling pushes harder into the same pool of people. Horizontal scaling finds new pools: new audiences, new countries, new placements, new angles or new traffic sources. When the vertical ladder stops working, this is where growth comes from.

d.s: New pools of people for the same offer

steps.say: Vertical scaling pushes harder into the same pool of people. Horizontal scaling finds new pools: new audiences, new countries, new placements, new angles, or new traffic sources. As the screen says, wider, not just deeper. When the vertical ladder stops working, this is where your growth comes from, the same offer reaching new people.

steps.p: Each lever opens a different pool of people. Most operators pull them in roughly this order, because the first ones are cheaper, faster to test and easier to undo.
steps.say: Here are five horizontal levers. Creatives, because new angles reach new people. Audiences, like broad, interests and lookalikes. Placements, such as feeds, stories and reels. Geos, meaning new countries. And sources, a new traffic platform. Each lever opens a different pool of people. Most operators pull them in roughly this order, because the first ones are cheaper, faster to test, and easier to undo.

steps.p: One winning idea feeds several new pools. Each branch is its own test with its own budget and rule card, but they all send people to the same honest lander and offer, and every result is judged on the network's confirmed postback.
steps.say: Look at this map. One winning ad set feeds several new pools: new angles, a broad audience, a Kenya test, and a second source. Each branch is its own test, with its own budget and its own rule card. Now follow the arrows. They all send clicks to the same honest lander, then on to the offer. And every result is judged on the network's postback for each confirmed F T D, first-time deposit.

steps.p: Rough guide, varies by account and vertical. New geos and new sources cost the most to test because almost everything has to be relearned, from creative to payment habits.
steps.say: Here's a rough guide to cost and risk by lever. A new angle, a new audience or a new placement are all low cost to test. You relearn the hook, who responds, or the format and size. A new geo is medium to high cost, because you relearn language, law and payments. And a new source is high cost, because you relearn the whole platform. That's why new geos and new sources are the most expensive tests. This varies by account and vertical.

steps.p: Illustration: CPA by week with one creative running alone versus a steady flow of new creatives. As the same people see the same ad, results fade. New creatives keep reaching fresh people.
steps.say: This is an illustration of C P A, cost per acquisition, by week. Look at the line for one creative running alone. It climbs from twenty dollars to forty four by week seven. As the same people see the same ad, results fade. Now the other line, a steady flow of new creatives. It stays around twenty to twenty three. New creatives keep reaching fresh people, so your creative supply matters as much as your budget.

steps.p: Example rule: plan one new creative per week for every $100 of daily spend. At $500 a day, that is five new creatives a week. If one in five usually wins, you get about one new winner each week.

d.label: new creatives a week at $500/day
d.note: Example rule, not a standard. Set your own from your hit rate.

steps.more: Work backwards from your own hit rate. If one in eight creatives becomes a winner and you need one new winner a week to replace fatigued ads, you need about eight new creatives a week. The bigger the spend, the faster the audience sees everything, so creative supply often limits scale before budget does. How to test them fairly: Creative testing lab module.
steps.say: Here's an example rule, not a standard. Plan one new creative per week for every hundred dollars of daily spend. At five hundred a day, that's five new creatives a week, the number on screen. If one in five usually wins, you get about one new winner each week. Better still, work backwards from your own hit rate. If one in eight wins and you need one new winner a week, you need about eight. The bigger the spend, the faster the audience sees everything, so creative supply often limits scale before budget does.

steps.p: Before you brief new creatives for a new pool or geo, look at what is already running there. Use research for ideas about angles and formats, never to copy another advertiser's ad, words or footage.

d.why: See which angles and formats are running in a new geo before you brief your own creatives; ideas only, never copies.

steps.say: Before you brief new creatives for a new pool or geo, look at what's already running there. This is where a tool like Spyvoo fits. It lets you see which angles and formats are running in a new geo before you brief your own creatives. Use research for ideas about angles and formats only. Never copy another advertiser's ad, words or footage.

steps.p: On many platforms, at the time of writing, broad targeting with strong creative and a clean conversion signal often matches or beats narrow interest targeting. This varies by account and changes over time; test both rather than assuming, and check the current Ads Manager.
steps.say: Narrow targeting versus broad. On the left, narrow interests: small, specific pools that fill up quickly. They're useful for new angles, but can cost more per result. On the right, broad: large pools that rely on your conversion data, where the creative does the targeting, and you need a clean signal. On many platforms, at the time of writing, broad with strong creative often matches or beats narrow. But this varies by account and changes over time. Test both rather than assuming, and check the current Ads Manager.

steps.p: Move geo by geo, starting with the one closest to what already works. Similar language, devices and payment methods reduce what you have to relearn.
steps.say: Here's how to expand to a new geo. Follow the steps. Prove the home geo first. Pick a close neighbour. Check the offer and the law. Localise the creative. Run a small test budget. Then scale with the ladder. Move geo by geo, starting with the one closest to what already works. Similar language, devices and payment methods reduce what you have to relearn.

steps.p: Example figures only. A higher payout does not always mean a better geo, because costs are often higher too. Compare margin per FTD and headroom, not the payout on its own.
steps.more: Check the maths: Geo A (30 − 18) ÷ 30 = 40%. Geo B (40 − 28) ÷ 40 = 30%. Geo C (55 − 50) ÷ 55 = 9%. Geo A and Geo B both earn $12 per FTD, but Geo A has more headroom to scale. Geo C has the biggest payout and the worst position: almost any cost rise makes it unprofitable.
steps.say: Here's a worked example comparing geos, with example figures only. Geo A pays thirty, with an eighteen dollar C P A, so forty percent headroom. Geo B pays forty, with a twenty eight dollar C P A, so thirty percent. Geo C pays fifty five, but its C P A is fifty, so only nine percent. Geo A and Geo B both earn twelve dollars per F T D, but A has more room to scale. And Geo C, with the biggest payout, is in the worst position. A higher payout doesn't always mean a better geo. Compare margin and headroom.

steps.h: Every geo gets its own numbers
steps.p: Example: Kenya pays $30 per FTD and you keep the 25% margin. Work out every line again from the new payout; never reuse the home geo's numbers. Starting rules from the Budget and kill rules module; adapt them to your vertical and data.
steps.say: Every geo gets its own numbers. Example: Kenya pays thirty dollars per F T D and you keep the twenty five percent margin. The target C P A is twenty two dollars fifty. The test budget per ad set is two to three times target, so forty five to sixty seven fifty. The zero-F T D kill is forty five. The C P A kill line is the lower of one point five times target and the payout, so thirty. And the scale line is eighteen. Work out every line again from the new payout, and never reuse the home geo's numbers. These are starting rules, so adapt them.

steps.p: Work out the new geo's target CPA from its own payout before you spend there. A lower payout moves every line down, including both kill lines. Then try a $36 payout and see how far the target moves.

steps.p: Treat every new country as a new launch, not as a copy of the old one. Run this list before you spend a single dollar there, and keep the answers in your notes.
d: Offer accepts traffic from this geo
Payout and cap for this geo are confirmed
Product is legal to advertise here

steps.p: Trading, gambling and finance ads usually need platform authorization, and rules are set country by country. Approval in one country does not carry to another. Full detail: Compliance for finance, trading and gambling offers module.

d.text: Check the platform's current policy and the local law for each new geo before you run. If you cannot get authorization, do not run there.

steps.p: Example: an ad that works in Nigeria in English may need Swahili, or English with local references, in Kenya, and French in much of Cameroon. Money amounts, payment methods and faces should match the viewer.

d.text: Show amounts in local currency and use real local payment names the offer supports.

Money amounts, payment methods and faces should all match the viewer. As the example on screen says, show amounts in local currency, and use real local payment names the offer supports.

steps.p: Opening new pools goes wrong in predictable ways. Each mistake on the left makes a new geo or audience look worse, or riskier, than it really is. Use the fixes on the right before you judge any new lever.

b.title: Fixes
items: Work out each geo's own numbers
Check policy and law per country

steps.say: Opening new pools goes wrong in predictable ways. Reusing the home geo's target, fixed by working out each geo's own numbers. Translating word for word, fixed by localising money, faces and payments. Assuming authorization carries over, fixed by checking policy and law per country. And testing four levers at once, fixed by testing one lever per test. Each mistake makes a new geo or audience look worse, or riskier, than it really is.

steps.h: Horizontal growth is slower and sturdier
steps.p: Each new pool takes time to open, but a business spread over several audiences, geos and sources does not collapse when one of them changes. That is the real reason to scale horizontally.

d.s: One audience changing should not end the business

steps.say: Horizontal growth is slower, and sturdier. Each new pool takes time to open. But a business spread over several audiences, geos and sources doesn't collapse when one of them changes. As the screen says, many pools, less fragility. One audience changing should not end the business. That's the real reason to scale horizontally.

lessons.title: Protecting ROI while you scale
objectives: By the end you can find the budget where profit peaks, not where spend peaks.
By the end you can set guardrails and rollback rules before you scale.
By the end you can reconcile platform and network numbers before making a scaling decision.

steps.p: Spend is easy to grow. Profit is what pays the team and funds the next test. Every scaling decision should answer one question: does this step increase total profit, after the network confirms the results?

d.b: Spend is a cost. Profit is the goal.
d.s: Bigger budgets can mean smaller profits

steps.say: Here's the core idea: spend is a cost, profit is the goal. Spend is easy to grow. Profit is what pays the team and funds the next test. So every scaling decision should answer one question. Does this step increase total profit, after the network confirms the results? Keep in mind, bigger budgets can mean smaller profits.

steps.p: Keep this formula in front of you on every scaling decision. Use confirmed results and the payout the network actually pays, after any adjustments, holds or rejected conversions.
steps.say: Keep this profit line in front of you on every scaling decision. Confirmed F T Ds, that's first-time deposits, times the payout, minus spend, equals profit. Use confirmed results, and the payout the network actually pays, after any adjustments, holds or rejected conversions. Not the numbers a dashboard estimates, but the money that actually arrives.

steps.p: Example with a $45 payout. As budget rises, CPA rises too. Total profit grows at first, then flattens, then falls. Spend kept growing the whole time.
steps.more: Check the maths. $200 ÷ $20 = 10 FTDs, revenue 10 × 45 = $450, profit $250. $400 ÷ $25 = 16 FTDs, revenue $720, profit $320. $800 ÷ $32 = 25 FTDs, revenue $1,125, profit $325. $1,200 ÷ $40 = 30 FTDs, revenue $1,350, profit $150. Going from $400 to $800 doubled spend and risk for $5 more profit a day.
steps.say: Here's a worked example with a forty five dollar payout. At two hundred dollars a day, the C P A, cost per acquisition, is twenty, giving ten F T Ds and two hundred and fifty dollars profit a day. At four hundred, C P A twenty five, sixteen F T Ds, three hundred and twenty profit. At eight hundred, C P A thirty two, twenty five F T Ds, three hundred and twenty five profit. At twelve hundred, C P A forty, thirty F T Ds, and profit falls to one hundred and fifty. Spend kept growing. Profit grew, flattened, then fell.

steps.p: Example from the table. Each bar is daily profit. The best risk-adjusted budget here is around $400 a day, not $1,200, because $800 doubles spend and risk for almost nothing.
steps.say: Here's the same example as bars. Each bar is daily profit. Two hundred and fifty at two hundred a day. Three hundred and twenty at four hundred. Three hundred and twenty five at eight hundred, barely any longer. And then look at the drop, one hundred and fifty at twelve hundred a day. The best risk-adjusted budget here is around four hundred a day, not twelve hundred, because eight hundred doubles spend and risk for almost nothing.

steps.h: The rule card agrees with the profit table
steps.p: Example: the same $45 payout with a 25% margin gives a target of $33.75 and a scale line of $27. Read the profit table again through the rule card. It stops the steps at about the same place the profit table does. Starting rules; adapt them.
steps.more: Check the maths: 45 × 0.75 = 33.75. 0.8 × 33.75 = 27. At $800 a day the $32 CPA is above the scale line, so no more steps. At $1,200 the $40 CPA is above the $33.75 target, so the stop rules send you back to the last budget that worked. The real rule card uses CPA since each step; here we use the table's averages to keep the example short. Full rules: Budget and kill rules module.
steps.say: Now read the profit table through the rule card. Example: the same forty five dollar payout with a twenty five percent margin gives a target of thirty three seventy five, and a scale line of twenty seven. At two hundred and four hundred a day, C P A is under twenty seven, so you step. At eight hundred, a thirty two dollar C P A is above the scale line, so keep, no more steps. At twelve hundred, forty is above target, so back to the last good budget. The rule card stops you at about the same place the profit table does. These are starting rules, so adapt them.

steps.p: Example: the extra $400 a day bought 9 extra FTDs. That is $44.44 per extra FTD against a $45 payout. The new money is almost exactly breaking even, which is why profit barely moved.
steps.say: Let's check the marginal C P A from four hundred to eight hundred a day. Example: the extra four hundred dollars a day bought nine extra F T Ds. That's forty four dollars forty four per extra F T D, the number on screen, against a forty five dollar payout. The new money is almost exactly breaking even. That's why profit barely moved, even though spend doubled.

steps.p: The ad platform and the network rarely agree on the numbers. Scale on what the network confirms and pays, because that is your actual revenue, not what the dashboard estimates.
steps.more: Gaps come from attribution windows, duplicate events, users who registered but did not qualify, and timing. Some gap is normal. A growing gap is a warning sign about tracking or traffic quality. Reconcile weekly and use the network figure for decisions.

On the right, the network confirms: spend six hundred, twenty four qualified F T Ds, C P A twenty five, and headroom smaller than it looked. Gaps come from attribution windows, duplicate events, users who registered but didn't qualify, and timing. Some gap is normal, but a growing gap is a warning sign about tracking or traffic quality. Scale on what the network confirms and pays, because that's your actual revenue.

steps.p: Once a week, put platform and network numbers side by side for each campaign and work out the match rate. Decide on the network column. A campaign whose match rate suddenly drops gets a tracking check, not a budget step. Full setup: Tracking setup lab module.
steps.more: Match rate is network-confirmed results divided by platform-reported results. Example: 24 ÷ 30 = 80%. NG_DEMO_SCALE at 50% is the one to investigate first: either tracking is double-counting or the traffic is not qualifying. Do not step its budget until you know which.

steps.p: Write these rules down before you raise budget. Rules written in advance are much easier to follow than decisions made while you watch money leave the account in real time.
d: Kill rule|spend limit with no result
Rollback rule|when to drop one step
Frequency watch|when the audience is tired
steps.say: Write these guardrails down before you raise budget. A kill rule, a spend limit with no result. A rollback rule, when to drop one step. A step limit, the maximum increase per day. A frequency watch, for when the audience is tired. And a quality check, weekly network feedback. Rules written in advance are much easier to follow than decisions made while you watch money leave the account in real time.

steps.p: Rolling back is not failure. It is how you find the real ceiling of a campaign without losing a week of profit trying to force it past that ceiling.
d: CPA since step above target 48 h
steps.say: Here's a rollback routine. If C P A since the step stays above target for forty eight hours, drop to the last good budget. Wait forty eight hours. Check the network data. Then resume the ladder, or hold. Rolling back isn't failure. It's how you find the real ceiling of a campaign, without losing a week of profit trying to force it past that ceiling.

steps.p: These mistakes turn a profitable campaign into a busy, unprofitable one. Each looks reasonable on the day, which is why the fixes need to be written as rules before you start scaling.

b.title: Fixes
items: Hold at the peak, grow sideways

steps.say: These mistakes turn a profitable campaign into a busy, unprofitable one. Scaling on platform numbers, fixed by deciding on network-confirmed data. Judging on average C P A only, fixed by checking marginal C P A each step. Pushing past the profit peak, fixed by holding at the peak and growing sideways. And no cash reserve for holds, fixed by reserving one payout cycle. Each mistake looks reasonable on the day, which is why the fixes need to be written as rules before you start.

steps.p: Once a week, step back from the daily noise and answer these questions using confirmed network data. Write the answers down so next week's review can compare against them.
steps.say: Once a week, step back from the daily noise and answer these questions using confirmed network data. Profit by campaign this week. The marginal C P A of each step. The gap between platform and network. Cap usage and payout dates. Creatives near fatigue. And next week's budget plan. Write the answers down, so next week's review can compare against them.

steps.d: The day I stopped asking how much I could spend and started asking what the last hundred dollars bought, my scaling stopped breaking.

steps.p: Scaling increases the cash you have tied up while you wait for payouts, and any hold or reversal from the network hits much harder at larger volume.

d.text: Do not scale with money you need for rent, salaries or tax. Keep a reserve that covers at least one full payout cycle at the new budget.

steps.p: Every campaign has a budget where profit peaks. Finding it is a success. Hold there, protect it and use horizontal levers to grow beyond it.

d.b: Find the peak, then hold it
d.s: Grow past it with new pools, not more pressure

steps.say: Here's the closing idea: find the peak, then hold it. Every campaign has a budget where profit peaks. Finding it is a success, not a failure. Hold there, protect it, and use horizontal levers to grow beyond it. Grow past the ceiling with new pools, not more pressure.

exam.q: You plan to grow from $150 to $600 a day. The network pays about 45 days after spend. How much more cash will be tied up than now?
Three geos: A payout $30, CPA $20. B payout $50, CPA $42. C payout $25, CPA $15. Which is the best scaling candidate on headroom?
exam.why: A 33%, B 16%, C 40%. C has the most buffer.

exam.q: Target $30. Two days after a +20% step, CPA since the step is $28 on 5 confirmed FTDs. What does the starting rule say?
options: Keep the budget; no more steps for now
Back to the last good budget
exam.why: $28 is above the $24 scale line but under the $30 target, so Keep: no change, and no more steps until CPA since the step returns to the scale line.

exam.q: An original at $100/day has $20 CPA. A duplicate, started at its $50 start budget, has $25 CPA. What is the blended CPA?
Budget levels with payout $40: $300 at $20 CPA, $600 at $30 CPA, $900 at $36 CPA. Where is profit highest?
Spend is $1,000 a day across 2 creatives that are fatiguing. Your hit rate is one in five. You need two new winners a week. What is the bottleneck?
options: Creative supply: you need about 10 new creatives a week
exam.why: Two winners at one in five needs around 10 new creatives a week. Without them, scale stalls.

exam.q: Platform shows $25 CPA. Network confirms $33 CPA. Payout $36. The gap has grown each week. What first?
options: Investigate tracking and traffic quality before any increase
Scale, the platform says it is profitable
exam.why: A growing gap signals tracking or quality issues, and confirmed headroom is only 8%. Fix before scaling.

exam.q: New geo test: payout $30, margin 25%. An ad set has spent $46 with 0 confirmed FTDs. What do you do?
options: Raise the budget to find buyers
Kill: spend passed the $45 zero-FTD line, 2 × $22.50
Copy it into a second ad set
exam.why: Each geo gets its own numbers. Target is $30 × 0.75 = $22.50, so the zero-FTD kill line is $45.
